items.english: It must have been exactly noon. The dogs too, perhaps sunk in their midday doze, were not heard to bark once. The hemp and millet ringing the threshing-yard shone their green leaves in the sun and stood hushed and perfectly still. And the sky seen beyond them, all stifling heat, trailed a shimmering haze, so that one might have doubted whether even the towering clouds were panting in this drought. Look where one would, nothing seemed to breathe but these three men. And those three kept their silence like the clay images enshrined in the Guandi Temple. . . .
notes: Kept the held tableau in short past stative sentences; rendered Kan-teibyou as Guandi Temple as a proper noun without explaining the deity, and the panting clouds as the narrator's conjecture.

items.english: Of course, this is no tale of Japan. — It is what happened one summer on the threshing-yard of the Liu family at a place called Changshan in China.
notes: Kept Changshan in pinyin; the text glosses it Chozan.

items.english: The man lying naked in the blazing sun was the master of this threshing-yard, surnamed Liu and named Dacheng, one of the leading men of fortune in Changshan. This man's one indulgence was drink, and from morning on he was scarcely ever parted from the cup. And that, "whenever he drank alone, he finished a whole jar," was a measure beyond ordinary men. Though, as already said, "three hundred mu of fields by the city wall, half planted with millet," so there was not the least fear that drink would burden his estate.
notes: Kept both tags visibly quoted and stiffly quantitative as borrowed Chinese, and left mu and jar unconverted for the pseudo-record measure.
